# Draft:Making a Killing (film)

Making a Killing: Reconciliation, Genocide and the Plunder of Canada is a 2025 Canadian documentary film produced by OneBC, a provincial political party in British Columbia. The film challenges widely accepted narratives about unmarked graves at former Canadian Indian residential schools and criticises contemporary reconciliation policy and legislation in Canada, in particular the implementation of the United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples (UNDRIP) and British Columbia’s Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples Act (DRIPA).
The film was released online by OneBC in early December 2025 and screened at an event at the British Columbia Legislative Assembly. It has attracted significant controversy for its treatment of residential school history and reconciliation, and has been condemned by critics as anti-Indigenous and revisionist, while supporters describe it as a challenge to what they consider to be an exaggerated or unproven narrative around mass graves in Kamloops and other sites.
Synopsis
Making a Killing centres on the emergence, political reception and consequences of claims about unmarked graves and alleged mass killings at former Indian residential schools, focusing in particular on the 2021 announcement by Tk’emlúps te Secwépemc First Nation regarding ground-penetrating radar (GPR) surveys at the site of the former Kamloops Indian Residential School.
Through interviews with academics, commentators, political figures and individuals identified as members of Indigenous communities, the film argues that:
* GPR results at some former residential school sites have been misrepresented as confirmed mass graves or mass murder without sufficient forensic evidence;
* federal and provincial governments, churches, universities and media have accepted these claims uncritically, contributing to a narrative of genocide that the film characterises as overstated or false;
* a taxpayer-funded “reconciliation industry” has developed, involving consultants, legal settlements, government programs and institutional initiatives which the filmmakers claim benefit a relatively small number of people while leaving many Indigenous people in poverty;
* legislative measures such as UNDRIP implementation and DRIPA have, in the view of the film, shifted power over land and resources in ways that undermine individual property rights and democratic accountability.
The documentary intercuts these interviews with footage from the British Columbia Legislature, scenes from communities in the province, and archival material about residential schools, public commemorations, and reconciliation ceremonies.
Production
The film was produced by members of the OneBC caucus after the party’s formation in 2025. According to the party’s promotional material, Making a Killing was intended to document what they describe as “the reconciliation industry” and to question commonly accepted claims about residential schools and genocide in Canada.
Filming took place in multiple locations across British Columbia, including Kamloops, Victoria and other communities where debates over reconciliation policy, land acknowledgements and Indigenous rights have been prominent. The production features interviews with commentators including political scientist Tom Flanagan and former Mount Royal University professor Frances Widdowson, among others, who have previously written critically about Indigenous policy and residential school narratives.
Release
The documentary was screened at the British Columbia Legislature on 1 December 2025 at an event hosted by OneBC caucus members. It was subsequently released for free streaming on the film’s official website and on video-sharing platforms in early December 2025. OneBC and its supporters promoted the film on social media as a feature-length exposé of what they describe as false genocide narratives and financially lucrative reconciliation programs.
Themes
Commentators have described Making a Killing as a political documentary that combines scepticism toward residential school unmarked-grave claims with a broader critique of reconciliation policy and identity-based politics in Canada.
The film advances the view that:
* narratives of genocide and mass murder at residential schools have been amplified without adequate evidentiary standards;
* government-funded reconciliation efforts and Indigenous rights legislation risk creating a “two-tier” system that privileges collective or group rights over individual liberties and equal citizenship;
* public symbols such as orange shirts and flags associated with residential school remembrance are, in the words of OneBC politicians quoted in other contexts, used to reinforce what they regard as false or exaggerated claims about Canada’s history.
These positions have placed the film within an existing current of criticism of reconciliation processes and unmarked-grave reporting, and have been widely rejected by Indigenous leaders, residential school survivors and many historians.
Reception
Support and positive commentary
Supportive commentators aligned with OneBC or with other critics of mainstream reconciliation narratives have welcomed the film as a challenge to what they consider to be an unquestioned consensus. An opinion piece in the Western Standard described the documentary as an explanation of a “strange episode of hysteria” surrounding unmarked-grave claims, and urged viewers to watch the film as a corrective to what the author saw as media and political exaggeration.
Rebel News covered the film positively, calling it “fact-driven” and arguing that it exposes a lucrative, taxpayer-funded reconciliation system. Supporters have also promoted the film on social media and alternative media platforms, characterising it as an example of political courage in raising questions about residential schools and Indigenous policy.
Criticism
The documentary has been widely criticised by opponents, including Indigenous representatives and commentators across the political spectrum, who argue that it downplays or denies the harms of the residential school system and contributes to anti-Indigenous sentiment. A column in The Islands Grapevine referred to OneBC leader Dallas Brodie as “promoting a documentary” that portrays what it calls the “reconciling industry” as a lucrative guilt campaign, and quoted former BC Green MLA Adam Olsen as saying that he feels for Indigenous people whose history is being questioned “in such a mean-spirited way”.
Critics have described the film as revisionist and insensitive toward survivors and families affected by residential schools, and have linked it to earlier controversies involving OneBC figures and comments about residential school survivors.
Political response
According to Rebel News, members of the governing British Columbia New Democratic Party (BC NDP) condemned the film, and Premier David Eby’s government indicated it was open to reviewing or changing rules around the use of public caucus funds for projects such as documentary films, in response to concerns that Making a Killing had been created using public money.
Coverage of the controversy around the film has formed part of a broader discussion in British Columbia politics over freedom of expression, responsible use of public funds by caucuses and political parties, and the appropriate way to handle disagreements over residential school history and reconciliation.
